title: The Infinitive
description: The present and aorist infinitives, the articular infinitive, indirect discourse and proper names.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html: The infinitive is a verbal noun. Like the subjunctive, its tenses show kind of action, not time; its negative is μή. Its subject, when expressed, is in the accusative: δεῖ αὐτὸν ἀπελθεῖν, it is necessary for him to go away. With the neuter article it is used like a noun in any case: διὰ τὸ εἶναι αὐτὸν ἐκεῖ, because he was there; μετὰ τὸ ἐγερθῆναι τὸν κύριον, after the Lord had been raised; πρὸ τοῦ βληθῆναι, before he was cast; ἐν τῷ λέγειν με, while I was saying; εἰς τὸ σωθῆναι αὐτούς, in order that they might be saved.

blocks.caption: Infinitives of λύω
rows: The second aorist infinitives are λιπεῖν (active, accented on the ending) and λιπέσθαι (middle). The infinitive of εἰμί is εἶναι. The first aorist active infinitive accents the next-to-last syllable: λῦσαι, πιστεῦσαι.

blocks.caption: Indirect discourse
blocks.html: Indirect statements usually take ὅτι with the indicative, keeping the tense of the direct words: εἶπεν ὅτι βλέπει τοὺς ἀνθρώπους, he said that he saw the men (his words were "I see"). English moves the verb into the past; Greek does not.

blocks.caption: Proper names
blocks.html: Proper names often take the article: ὁ Ἰησοῦς. Ἰησοῦς has Ἰησοῦ in the genitive, dative and vocative and Ἰησοῦν in the accusative. Some nouns naming something unique are used with or without the article: θεός or ὁ θεός, πνεῦμα or τὸ πνεῦμα, κόσμος, νόμος.

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: λύεσθαι is both middle and passive; in the aorist λύσασθαι is middle and λυθῆναι passive. With δεῖ and ἔξεστιν the person goes in the accusative (δεῖ αὐτόν) and the dative (ἔξεστίν σοι) respectively.
